questions.q: Define "imagery" (बिंब) and "metaphor" (रूपक) in your own words, and give one original example of each that is NOT from the textbook.
questions.a: Imagery: Language that activates the five senses to create a concrete mental picture (e.g., "The kitchen smelled of cumin and burnt onions, and the pressure cooker hissed like an angry snake"). Metaphor: A direct equation between two unlike things to transfer meaning (e.g., "Her silence was a locked room with no keyhole"). A wrong answer that confuses metaphor with simile ("Her silence was like a locked room") reveals the student has not internalised the "absence of comparative particles" rule; a wrong answer that lists only visual imagery reveals a narrow sensory repertoire.

questions.q: In the poem, the phrase "डक्यस डक्यस" (dark dark) appears repeatedly. Is this primarily an auditory image, a visual image, or a metaphor? Justify your classification in two sentences.
questions.a: "डक्यस डक्यस" is primarily a **visual image** (दृश्य बिंब) because it forces the reader to see the girl's skin colour through insistent repetition; it becomes a metaphor only when the poet later equates that darkness with "ignorance" or "social stigma" in the lines where Paik says "रके दक्न घ क्क्षन्क् क्से" (they consider this darkness a flaw). A student who calls it only a metaphor misses the sensory grounding; a student who calls it only auditory confuses the phonetic repetition (alliteration) with the sense appealed to.

questions.q: The poem contains the line: "पैक लूँज ध यम्ढ गे" (Paik is the threshold's Yama). Identify the tenor and the vehicle, then explain what quality of Yama is transferred to Paik in this context.
questions.a: Tenor (उपमेय) = Paik; Vehicle (उपमान) = Yama (god of death/threshold guardian). The transferred quality is **inescapable authority at the boundary** — just as Yama decides who enters the afterlife, Paik's literacy decides who enters the world of written power. A wrong answer that says "Yama means death, so Paik brings death" shows literalism and ignores the "threshold guardian" aspect; a wrong answer that swaps tenor/vehicle reveals confusion about the direction of metaphorical transfer.

questions.q: Compare the tactile imagery in "बुढ़ हक्क न्कोकोन्ह :ेक्फुर् ल्स् एक्द्र ग्स र्फ्क्क म्ल्दक ब्क्व ब्स्ब क्को ध त्केउ् ल्स् त्क्म्क ग्क्व्क" (Old language sticks to the tongue like dry roti) with the visual metaphor "पैक पक्सिक्सा द्क्स य्स्द्ज प्जोक्ग्ह द्जुस त्क्र्ह गे" (Paik wants to catch letters like butterflies). What does the shift from tactile to visual suggest about Paik's evolving relationship with language?
questions.a: The tactile image (dry roti sticking) conveys **resistance and discomfort** — the old oral tradition is coarse, unyielding, and physically burdensome. The visual metaphor (catching letters like butterflies) conveys **agency, delight, and fragility** — literacy is something Paik actively pursues, finds beautiful, but must handle gently. The shift signals her movement from passive victim of tradition to active architect of her future. A student who only lists the two devices without contrasting their thematic function misses the analytical demand of the question.

questions.q: Critique the following student interpretation: "The metaphor 'पैक वीएनह गे' (Paik is a bird) means she is free and happy." Is this reading adequate? Why or why not?
questions.a: The reading is **inadequate** because it ignores the immediate context: "पैक वीएनह गे / पप्य गे / उ व [क व ह्ख गे / ध्खे ध्खे म्खेके द्ज्र्ह गे" (Paik is a bird / fragile / sometimes she trembles / sometimes she gives a shock like lightning). The metaphor carries **ambivalence** — bird suggests flight/freedom BUT also fragility ("पप्य") and sudden, startling power ("दक्ख्क्ष क्क्ष क्से"). A defensible interpretation must hold both freedom and vulnerability together. A student who offers only the positive reading demonstrates "cherry-picking" evidence, a common Board-exam error.

questions.q: Write a four-line stanza (in Hindi or English) that uses at least two distinct sensory images and one metaphor to describe a child learning to read under a streetlamp at night. Label each device in brackets.
questions.a:
Example:  
"पीली रोशनी में अक्षर नाचते [visual image: पीली रोशनी, नाचते]  
ठंडी हवा पन्ने फड़फड़ाती [tactile image: ठंडी हवा, फड़फड़ाती]  
उसकी उँगलियाँ जुगनू हैं [metaphor: उँगलियाँ = जुगनू — small, self-generated light in darkness]  
अंधेरा हार मानता है।"  
A poor answer would use only visual images, or use a simile ("उँगलियाँ जुगनू जैसी हैं") instead of a metaphor, or fail to label devices — indicating the student cannot yet distinguish or deploy the tools independently.
